surface_summary: Miss Susan Baird is found dead in her locked library, apparently poisoned by prussic acid on a peach. Suspicion falls on various relatives and acquaintances, including Kitty Baird, her niece and heir, and Major Leigh Wallace, a suitor. The investigation uncovers family secrets, forged wills, and a complex web of motives.
accepted_facts: Miss Susan Baird died from prussic acid poisoning administered on a peach.
The house was locked from the outside with the key left in the front door.
Kitty Baird inherited a large fortune from her aunt, previously unknown to her.
Charles Craige had financial troubles and was close to Miss Susan Baird.
inferred_conclusions: Kitty Baird murdered her aunt to inherit the fortune.
Major Leigh Wallace was responsible due to jealousy and family disputes.
Mrs. Amos Parsons was involved in the murder to gain blackmail material.
mechanism_description: Charles Craige, driven by financial desperation and to cover up his forgery, poisoned Miss Susan Baird by applying prussic acid to one side of a fruit knife used to cut a peach. He ensured only Miss Baird ate the poisoned half by eating the safe side himself. He attempted to frame others by planting evidence and manipulating servants. He later killed Mrs. Parsons to silence her when she threatened exposure.
delivery_path: Craige applies prussic acid to one side of the fruit knife blade.
Craige cuts the peach and places the poisoned half for Miss Baird.
Miss Baird eats the poisoned half and dies within minutes.
Craige plants forged papers and the revolver in Rodgers' car to frame others.
Mrs. Parsons attempts blackmail using stolen papers.
Craige kills Mrs. Parsons by spraying poison on the cat's paw to silence her.
Craige is caught and confesses after being confronted.
outcome_result: Charles Craige is arrested and confesses to the murder of Miss Susan Baird and Mrs. Parsons.

false_assumption.statement: Kitty Baird is the murderer who poisoned her aunt to inherit the fortune.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Kitty had a quarrel with her aunt shortly before the death and stood to gain a large inheritance. The revolver with her initials was found in the victim's car, suggesting involvement.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The revolver was planted by the real culprit, Charles Craige, to frame Kitty. The quarrel was unrelated to the murder, and Kitty was innocent.

supporting_points: Kitty quarreled with her aunt on the day of the murder.
Kitty inherited a large fortune from her aunt.
A revolver with Kitty's initials was found in the victim's car.
Kitty was seen entering the house with a package of peaches.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The revolver was planted and the evidence was manipulated by Charles Craige.

red_herrings.description: Major Leigh Wallace was suspected due to his quarrel with Miss Susan Baird and his presence with peaches at the house.
red_herrings.points_at_suspect: His agitation and presence at the house at the time of the murder.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He brought peaches as a peace offering and was not involved in the murder.

red_herrings.description: Mrs. Amos Parsons was suspected of blackmail and involvement in the murder due to her attempts to bribe Oscar and her suspicious behavior.
red_herrings.points_at_suspect: Her bribery attempts and possession of incriminating papers.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was trying to gain leverage but was ultimately killed by Craige to silence her.

closed_circle.rationale: All had access to the house, motives related to inheritance or personal interests, and were involved in the social circle around Miss Susan Baird.

inference_path.correction: The poison was deliberately applied to only one side to poison only Miss Baird.
inference_path.effect: Indicates a planned murder with knowledge of victim's eating habits.

inference_path.correction: The door was locked from outside to trap or exclude others.
inference_path.effect: Suggests the murderer locked the house to create a closed circle.

inference_path.effect: Reveals the murderer is willing to kill to cover tracks.

Observation of cat's injured paw and poison traces

inference_path.observation: Charles Craige had forged documents and financial troubles.
inference_path.correction: Craige had motive to kill to cover forgery and gain financially.
inference_path.effect: Identifies Craige as the murderer with strong motive and opportunity.
required_evidence: Forgery evidence from Holt will case

inference_path.observation: The rubber bulb syringe with poison was found missing and then returned.
inference_path.correction: Craige used the syringe to apply poison and Mrs. Parsons returned it to frame others.
inference_path.effect: Shows the use of syringe as murder weapon and framing device.

discriminating_test.design: Reenact the poisoning by applying poison to one side of a fruit knife and cutting a peach, then observing that only the person eating the poisoned side is affected. Test the accessibility of the Dutch door panel and the worn floorboards to confirm secret entry or exit. Examine the timing of Oscar's presence and the location of the poison syringe to confirm the sequence of events.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test reveals that the poison was deliberately applied to one side of the knife, that the Dutch door panel was used for secret access, and that Oscar's testimony about his whereabouts was false.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The reenactment confirms that only the person eating the poisoned half is affected, the Dutch door panel moves silently and is well used, and Oscar's presence at the house at 5 PM is confirmed by witness statements.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is provided with detailed descriptions of the locked house, the poison application, and the movements of key characters. The discovery of the poison only on one side of the knife, the secret Dutch door panel, and the forged will papers are all clues available to the reader. The false suspicions cast on Kitty and Wallace are supported by evidence but ultimately refuted by the confession and final revelations. The reader could solve the case by carefully analyzing the timing, access, and motives presented.
